prompt:
Let $A$ be a set of positive integers such that for any $x,y\in A$
$$x>y\implies x-y\ge\frac{xy}{25}.$$
Find the maximal possible number of elements of the set $A$.

solutions.title: Reciprocals are $\frac1{25}$ apart
solutions.body:
Dividing by $xy>0$, the condition reads
$$\frac1y-\frac1x\ge\frac1{25}\qquad\text{for all }x>y\text{ in }A .$$
Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\dots<a_n\}$. It suffices to require the condition for consecutive elements (the differences of reciprocals then add up), i.e.
$$\frac1{a_{i+1}}\le\frac1{a_i}-\frac1{25}=\frac{25-a_i}{25a_i}\qquad(1\le i<n).$$

**Upper bound.** If $a_i\ge25$, the right-hand side is $\le0$, so $a_i$ must be the largest element. If $a_i<25$, then
$$a_{i+1}\ge h(a_i),\qquad h(a)=\frac{25a}{25-a},$$
and $h$ is increasing on $[1,25)$. Since the $a_i$ are distinct positive integers, $a_5\ge5$. Then successively
$$a_6\ge h(5)=6.25\Rightarrow a_6\ge7,\qquad a_7\ge h(7)=\tfrac{175}{18}\approx9.7\Rightarrow a_7\ge10,$$
$$a_8\ge h(10)=\tfrac{50}{3}\approx16.7\Rightarrow a_8\ge17,\qquad a_9\ge h(17)=\tfrac{425}8\approx53.1\Rightarrow a_9\ge54 .$$
As $a_9\ge25$, there is no $a_{10}$. Hence $n\le9$.

**Example with 9 elements.** $A=\{1,2,3,4,5,7,10,17,54\}$. The consecutive differences of reciprocals are
$$\tfrac12,\ \tfrac16,\ \tfrac1{12},\ \tfrac1{20},\ \tfrac2{35},\ \tfrac3{70},\ \tfrac7{170},\ \tfrac{37}{918},$$
all $\ge\frac1{25}$ (e.g. $\frac{37}{918}\approx0.0403$, $\frac7{170}\approx0.0412$, $\frac3{70}\approx0.0429$). A computer search over all chains confirms that $9$ is the maximum.

**Answer: $9$.** ∎

prompt:
Prove that for any prime $p\ge5$, the number
$$\sum_{0<k<\frac{2p}{3}}\binom pk$$
is divisible by $p^2$.
answer: $\frac1p\binom pk\equiv\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}k\pmod p$, so it suffices that $\sum_{0<k<2p/3}\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}k=\sum_{p/3<k<2p/3}\frac1k\equiv0$, which follows from the symmetry $k\mapsto p-k$.

solutions.title: Reduce to harmonic sums modulo $p$
solutions.body:
All fractions below are elements of the field $\mathbb Z_p$ (denominators are $<p$).

**Step 1.** For $0<k<p$,
$$\binom pk=\frac pk\binom{p-1}{k-1},\qquad \binom{p-1}{k-1}=\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{p-j}{j}\equiv\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{-j}{j}=(-1)^{k-1}\pmod p .$$
Since $k\binom pk=p\binom{p-1}{k-1}$, the integer $\frac1p\binom pk=\frac1k\binom{p-1}{k-1}$ satisfies $\frac1p\binom pk\equiv\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k}\pmod p$. So the claim is equivalent to
$$S=\sum_{0<k<2p/3}\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k}\equiv0\pmod p .$$

**Step 2: rewrite $S$.** Let $m=\lfloor2p/3\rfloor$ and $H_r=\sum_{k=1}^r\frac1k$. Then
$$S=\sum_{k=1}^m\frac1k-2\sum_{2j\le m}\frac1{2j}=H_m-H_{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}.$$
If $p=3q+1$ then $m=2q$; if $p=3q+2$ then $m=2q+1$; in both cases $\lfloor m/2\rfloor=q=\lfloor p/3\rfloor$. Hence
$$S=\sum_{p/3<k<2p/3}\frac1k .$$

**Step 3: symmetry.** Since $p/3$ and $2p/3$ are not integers, $k\mapsto p-k$ maps the integers of the interval $(p/3,2p/3)$ bijectively onto themselves. Using $\frac1{p-k}\equiv-\frac1k$,
$$S=\sum_{p/3<k<2p/3}\frac1{p-k}\equiv-\sum_{p/3<k<2p/3}\frac1k=-S .$$
So $2S\equiv0$, and as $p$ is odd, $S\equiv0\pmod p$. Therefore $p^2$ divides $\sum_{0<k<2p/3}\binom pk$. (Check: $p=5$: $\binom51+\binom52+\binom53=5+10+10=25$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $n\ge2$ be a natural number. Prove that
$$\prod_{k=2}^n\ln k<\frac{\sqrt{n!}}{n}.$$
answer: Use $\ln x<\frac{x-1}{\sqrt x}$ for $x>1$ and multiply over $k=2,\dots,n$: $\prod\sqrt k\cdot\prod\frac{k-1}{k}=\frac{\sqrt{n!}}n$.

solutions.title: A termwise estimate
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** For $x>1$: $\ln x<\dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt x}$.

*Proof.* Put $x=t^2$, $t>1$; the claim becomes $2\ln t<t-\frac1t$. Let $g(t)=t-\frac1t-2\ln t$. Then $g(1)=0$ and
$$g'(t)=1+\frac1{t^2}-\frac2t=\Big(1-\frac1t\Big)^2>0\quad(t>1),$$
so $g(t)>0$ for $t>1$. $\square$

For $k=2,\dots,n$ we have $0<\ln k<\sqrt k\cdot\frac{k-1}{k}$. Multiplying these inequalities between positive numbers:
$$\prod_{k=2}^n\ln k<\prod_{k=2}^n\sqrt k\cdot\prod_{k=2}^n\frac{k-1}k=\sqrt{n!}\cdot\frac1n .$$
∎

solutions.title: Compare derivatives directly (official second solution)
solutions.body:
Let $f(x)=\ln x$ and $g(x)=\sqrt x\cdot\frac{x-1}x=\sqrt x-\frac1{\sqrt x}$. Then $f(1)=g(1)=0$ and
$$g'(x)-f'(x)=\frac1{2\sqrt x}+\frac1{2x\sqrt x}-\frac1x=\frac{x+1-2\sqrt x}{2x\sqrt x}=\frac{(\sqrt x-1)^2}{2x\sqrt x}>0\quad(x>1).$$
Hence $g-f$ is strictly increasing on $[1,\infty)$ and $g(x)>f(x)$ for $x>1$, i.e. $\ln k<\sqrt k\frac{k-1}k$ for $k\ge2$. Multiplying over $k=2,\dots,n$ and telescoping $\prod\frac{k-1}k=\frac1n$ gives the claim. ∎

prompt:
Let $A,B,C$ be nonempty sets in $\mathbb R^n$. Suppose that $A$ is bounded, $C$ is closed and convex, and $A+B\subseteq A+C$. Prove that $B\subseteq C$.

We remind that $E+F=\{e+f:e\in E,\ f\in F\}$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is convex iff $tx+(1-t)y\in D$ for all $x,y\in D$ and any $t\in[0,1]$.
answer: Fix $b\in B$, $a_0\in A$ and iterate $a_{i-1}+b=a_i+c_i$; then $b-\frac1i(c_1+\dots+c_i)=\frac{a_i-a_0}i\to0$, the averages lie in $C$ by convexity, and $C$ is closed. (Alternatively, separate $b\notin C$ from $C$ by a linear functional.)

solutions.title: Averaging (official)
solutions.body:
Fix $b\in B$ and $a_0\in A$. Since $a_0+b\in A+B\subseteq A+C$, there are $a_1\in A$, $c_1\in C$ with $a_0+b=a_1+c_1$. Repeating with $a_1$ in place of $a_0$, and so on, we get $a_i\in A$, $c_i\in C$ with
$$a_{i-1}+b=a_i+c_i\qquad(i=1,2,\dots).$$
Adding the first $i$ equations: $a_0+ib=a_i+c_1+\dots+c_i$, i.e.
$$b-x_i=\frac{a_i-a_0}{i},\qquad x_i=\frac{c_1+\dots+c_i}{i}.$$

A convex set contains all convex combinations of its points (induction on the number of points: $\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}\lambda_jc_j=(1-\lambda_{k+1})\sum_{j\le k}\frac{\lambda_j}{1-\lambda_{k+1}}c_j+\lambda_{k+1}c_{k+1}$ when $\lambda_{k+1}<1$). So $x_i\in C$.

$A$ is bounded, say $\|a\|\le M$ on $A$, so $\|b-x_i\|\le\frac{2M}i\to0$. Thus $x_i\to b$, and since $C$ is closed, $b\in C$. Hence $B\subseteq C$. ∎

solutions.title: Separating hyperplane
solutions.body:
Suppose some $b\in B$ is not in $C$. Since $C$ is nonempty, closed and convex, there is a linear functional $\varphi$ (e.g. $\varphi(x)=\langle b-c^*,x\rangle$ with $c^*$ the point of $C$ nearest to $b$) and a real $\delta>0$ with
$$\varphi(c)\le\varphi(b)-\delta\qquad\text{for all }c\in C .$$
$A$ is bounded, so $s=\sup_{a\in A}\varphi(a)$ is finite; pick $a_0\in A$ with $\varphi(a_0)>s-\delta$. Then $a_0+b\in A+B\subseteq A+C$, so $a_0+b=a+c$ with $a\in A$, $c\in C$, and
$$\varphi(a_0)+\varphi(b)=\varphi(a)+\varphi(c)\le s+\varphi(b)-\delta<\varphi(a_0)+\varphi(b),$$
a contradiction. Hence $B\subseteq C$. ∎
